title: The Magi, King Herod, and the Flight to Egypt
summary: Magi from the east follow a star to Jerusalem, asking where the newborn king of the Jews is, and King Herod, alarmed, learns from the scribes that the Messiah is to be born in Bethlehem. The Magi find the child, worship him, and present gold, frankincense, and myrrh, then return home by another route. Warned in a dream, Joseph flees with Mary and Jesus to Egypt while Herod massacres the boys of Bethlehem; after Herod's death the family settles in Nazareth in Galilee.
story:
Chapter 1 established who Jesus is: son of David, son of Abraham, Immanuel. Chapter 2 shows how the world receives him. Gentile foreigners come to worship; the reigning king of the Jews tries to kill him; and Jerusalem's religious experts know exactly where the Messiah should be born but do not go to see. Krister Stendahl summed up the two chapters as who and whence: chapter 1 answers who Jesus is, and chapter 2, built around place names, answers where he comes from and why he ends up in an obscure Galilean village.

Each place is tied to a prophecy, and together they trace Israel's history. Bethlehem is David's town; Egypt is the land of slavery and the exodus; Ramah is where the exiles were gathered for Babylon; Nazareth is a village no prophet named. The child relives his people's story: he goes down to Egypt and is called out again as God's son, as Israel was, and in the next two chapters he will pass through the waters of baptism and be tested forty days in the wilderness, as Israel was tested forty years. Where Israel failed, he will be faithful. The chapter also opens the Gospel's long contrast between two kinds of kingship, the fearful, violent rule of Herod and the rule of the child who will be crucified under the title King of the Jews (27:37).
historical:
Herod the Great was named king of Judea by the Roman Senate in 40 BC and took Jerusalem in 37 BC. He was an Idumean, from a people forcibly converted to Judaism by the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus, and many Jews never accepted him as a legitimate king of the Jews, the very title the Magi ask about. He was among the great builders of antiquity: he rebuilt the Jerusalem temple on a vast scale from about 20 BC, built the harbor city of Caesarea, and fortified Masada and the Herodium, near Bethlehem, where he was buried; Ehud Netzer announced the discovery of his tomb there in 2007. He was also pathologically suspicious. Josephus, writing in the 90s AD, records that he executed the former high priest Hyrcanus II, his wife Mariamne (29 BC), her mother, his sons Alexander and Aristobulus (about 7 BC), and his eldest son Antipater only days before his own death (Antiquities 17.187). As he lay dying he ordered the leading men of the nation shut in the hippodrome at Jericho and killed when he died, so that there would be mourning at his death; the order was not carried out (Antiquities 17.174-179). Josephus mentions an eclipse of the moon shortly before his death (Antiquities 17.167), which is one of the anchors for dating it to 4 BC.

No other ancient source mentions the killing of the boys of Bethlehem. Josephus, who catalogues Herod's crimes at length, is silent, and that silence is the main reason many historians doubt the event. Others note that Bethlehem was a village of perhaps a few hundred people, so that the boys under two may have numbered a dozen or two (the estimate of R. T. France, Novum Testamentum, 1979, and Paul Maier, 1998), a crime small enough to be lost among Herod's larger atrocities, and one that fits what Josephus says of him. The fifth-century Latin writer Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.4.11) records Augustus's joke that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son, which he connects with an order to kill boys under two in Syria, but the report is late, garbled, and probably influenced by Matthew.

After Herod's death Augustus divided the kingdom among three sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria, and Idumea as ethnarch, though Matthew uses the popular language of reigning. He began with a massacre of about three thousand people at Passover in the temple courts (Antiquities 17.213-218) and ruled so harshly that Augustus deposed him in AD 6 and banished him to Vienne in Gaul. Herod Antipas received Galilee and Perea, where he rebuilt Sepphoris, about four miles from Nazareth, and later founded Tiberias. Joseph's fear of Archelaus and his move to Galilee fit these facts. Egypt was a natural refuge: it lay outside Herod's power, and its Jewish population was very large; Philo of Alexandria claimed a million Jews in Egypt (Against Flaccus 43), and there was even a Jewish temple at Leontopolis, founded by the priest Onias IV in the second century BC.

Bethlehem, about six miles south of Jerusalem, was the home of Jesse and David (1 Samuel 17:12). By the middle of the second century Christians pointed to a cave there as the birthplace (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 78; Origen, Against Celsus 1.51), and Constantine built the Church of the Nativity over it in the 320s and 330s. Matthew says the Magi found the child in a house (verse 11), and Herod's order concerning boys two years old and under suggests that some months, perhaps more than a year, had passed since the birth.
cultural:
The Magi (magoi) were originally, according to Herodotus (Histories 1.101), one of the tribes of the Medes, a priestly caste who interpreted dreams at the Persian court (1.107-108). By this period the word covered Persian priests, sages and astrologers of the East, and also, less kindly, sorcerers and charlatans; the Greek translations of Daniel use it for the wise men of Babylon's court (Daniel 2:2), and Acts 13:6-8 uses it of the sorcerer Elymas. Philo (Special Laws 3.100) distinguished the true magic of the Persian sages, a study of nature, from mere wizardry. Matthew says only that they came from the east. Justin (Dialogue 78) thought of Arabia, the source of frankincense and myrrh; others of Persia or Babylon, the home of Babylonian astronomy. A real parallel exists: in AD 66 the Armenian king Tiridates, himself a magus according to Pliny (Natural History, book 30), came with magi to Rome to do homage to Nero and, according to Dio Cassius (Roman History, book 63), went home by a different route. The later tradition of three kings grew from the three gifts and from Psalm 72:10-11 and Isaiah 60:3-6, which speak of kings and nations bringing gold and frankincense; Tertullian (Against Marcion 3.13) called the Magi almost kings.

Ancient people widely believed that the heavens announced the births and deaths of rulers. Suetonius (Augustus 94) collects portents of Augustus's birth, and Tacitus (Annals 14.22) says a comet under Nero was taken to mean a change of ruler. Jewish readers had Balaam's oracle, “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17), read of a coming ruler in the Damascus Document (CD 7:18-21) and in a Qumran collection of messianic texts (4Q175); in the 130s AD Rabbi Akiva is said to have hailed the rebel leader Simon ben Kosiba as Bar Kokhba, son of the star (Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 4:8). The phrase the BSB translates ‘in the east’ (en tē anatolē, verses 2 and 9) can also mean ‘at its rising’, the astronomical term for a star's first appearance at dawn, and several modern versions translate it that way.

The gifts were the luxuries of the ancient world. Gold was royal tribute. Frankincense, a resin from Boswellia trees of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, was burned in the temple's incense (Exodus 30:34). Myrrh, a resin from Commiphora trees of the same regions, was used in perfume, medicine, anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), and burial; it will reappear in the wine offered at the cross (Mark 15:23) and the spices for Jesus' body (John 19:39). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.9.2) read the gifts as signs of what Jesus is: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who would die. Matthew himself does not interpret them.

Two further customs matter. Being warned in a dream (verses 12 and 22) uses a verb (chrēmatizō) often used for a divine instruction, and dreams were widely trusted as a channel of revelation, in Israel as among the Magi's own people. And Rachel's tomb stood in two traditions: Genesis 35:19 places it on the way to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem, while 1 Samuel 10:2 places it in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, the district of Ramah, which lay about five miles north of the city. Jeremiah's Ramah was also the place where the Babylonians gathered the exiles in chains before deporting them (Jeremiah 40:1). Matthew's quotation joins Bethlehem's grief to the grief of the exile.
literary:
The chapter is a narrative in four scenes, each built around a quotation from Scripture: the Magi and Herod (verses 1 to 12, Micah 5:2 combined with 2 Samuel 5:2), the flight to Egypt (verses 13 to 15, Hosea 11:1), the massacre (verses 16 to 18, Jeremiah 31:15), and the return and settlement in Nazareth (verses 19 to 23, ‘He will be called a Nazarene’). Dreams steer the action. The Magi are warned once (verse 12), and Joseph three more times (verses 13, 19, and 22), after his first dream in 1:20, and each time he obeys at once in words that echo the command: the angel's “Take the Child and His mother” (verses 13 and 20) is answered by he got up and took the child and his mother (verses 14 and 21). The action is directed from heaven while Herod plots on earth.

The story is built on contrasts. There are two kings: the one who has been born King of the Jews and the one who holds the title. There is false worship and true: Herod says he wants to worship (verse 8), while the Magi fall down and worship (verse 11). The chief priests and scribes know the Scriptures and do nothing, and foreigners who have only a star travel far and rejoice “with great delight” (verse 10). Jerusalem is troubled with Herod (verse 3), a detail that anticipates the city's rejection of Jesus. The title King of the Jews will not be heard again until the passion, where it is spoken only by Gentiles (27:11, 29, 37), and the Magi who worship at the start anticipate the nations who will be discipled at the end (28:19).

The Moses pattern is strong. Pharaoh killed Israel's baby boys and one child escaped (Exodus 1 and 2); here a king kills boys and one child escapes. The angel's words, “those seeking the Child's life are now dead” (verse 20), echo God's words to Moses, “all the men who sought to kill you are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Josephus's retelling of Moses' birth (Antiquities 2.205-216) adds that a sacred scribe warned Pharaoh of the birth of a deliverer and that God spoke to Moses' father Amram in a dream, details closer still to Matthew. Dale Allison (The New Moses, 1993) traces this typology through the whole Gospel. The fulfillment formulas also vary in a way that matters: at verses 15 and 23 the Greek uses purpose clauses (hina, hopōs, in order that it might be fulfilled), but at verse 17, of the massacre, Matthew writes simply “Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled” (tote, then), as he will again of Judas's blood money (27:9). He does not say the children died in order that Scripture be fulfilled.

outline.t: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem
Herod consults the scribes and sends the Magi to Bethlehem
The Magi worship the child and go home another way
Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
The return and the settling in Nazareth

doctrines.note: Jesus is born King of the Jews in David's town, the shepherd-ruler of Micah 5:2. Matthew sets his true kingship against Herod's violent, fearful kingship, and the title will return at the cross (27:37).

Four quotations show four kinds of fulfillment: a direct prediction of the Messiah's birthplace (Micah 5:2), a pattern in Israel's history completed in Israel's representative (Hosea 11:1), an image of grief carried into a new sorrow (Jeremiah 31:15), and a theme gathered from several prophets (verse 23). Matthew's fulfillment is wider than prediction.

God guides events through a star, dreams, and the timing of Herod's death, protecting the child without removing the danger. Providence here works through flight, exile, and a refugee family's obedience, and it does not prevent all evil; the massacre is Herod's act, and Matthew refuses to say it happened in order to fulfill Scripture.

The verb proskyneō, to bow down or worship, appears three times (verses 2, 8, and 11). The Magi's worship is costly, joyful, and physical: they travel, rejoice, fall down, and open their treasures. Herod's pretended worship shows that the word can be spoken by someone who means murder.

The first people in Matthew to worship Jesus are Gentiles from the east, fulfilling the picture of nations coming to Zion's light (Isaiah 60:3). The Gospel that ends with a command to make disciples of all nations begins with the nations coming to the king.

words.note: Magos, a Magus, a sage of the Persian priestly class, and more loosely a magician. It occurs six times in the New Testament, four in this chapter and twice in Acts 13:6-8 for the sorcerer Elymas. BDAG gives both senses. Judaism regarded astrology and magic with suspicion (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), which makes the Magi's role here striking: people outside Israel's covenant, using the means they had, are led by God to the Messiah, and then led further by Scripture (verses 5 and 6).

Astēr, star. It occurs 24 times in the New Testament, 14 of them in Revelation. Numbers 24:17 had spoken of a star coming out of Jacob, a text Jews of this period read of a coming ruler; Matthew does not quote it, but many readers think it stands behind his star. Matthew's star rises, goes ahead of the Magi, and stops over a place (verse 9), which is why interpreters from John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 6) onward have doubted that an ordinary star is meant.

Proskyneō, to bow down before, pay homage, worship. It occurs about 60 times in the New Testament, 13 in Matthew and 24 in Revelation. It can describe homage to a king, and so the Magi's intention may at first mean royal homage; but Matthew uses it again and again of people before Jesus (8:2, 14:33, 28:9, 28:17), and in 4:10 Jesus says, quoting Deuteronomy, that it belongs to God alone. The Gospel's first worshipers are here.

Poimainō, to shepherd, tend, rule. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament. Matthew's quotation joins Micah 5:2 to God's words to David, “You will shepherd My people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2), so that the ruler from Bethlehem is a shepherd-king like David. Shepherd was an ancient title for kings, and the prophets condemned Israel's rulers as false shepherds (Ezekiel 34). Matthew's Jesus will have compassion on crowds like sheep without a shepherd (9:36) and will be struck as the shepherd (26:31).

Anachōreō, to withdraw, go away, take refuge. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament, ten in Matthew, and four of them in this chapter (verses 12, 13, 14, and 22). It becomes a pattern in the Gospel: faced with a threat, Jesus withdraws (4:12, 12:15, 14:13), not from fear but because his hour has not come. The Messiah's first movements are those of a refugee.

Plēroō, to fill, fulfill, complete. It occurs about 87 times in the New Testament and 16 in Matthew, where it carries the formula this happened to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet. In Matthew fulfillment means that a text reaches its fullness in Jesus, whether as a prediction come true, a pattern completed, or a hope realized; Jesus uses the same verb when he says he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (5:17).

Nazōraios, Nazarene. It occurs thirteen times in the New Testament, seven in Acts, where Christians are called the sect of the Nazarenes (Acts 24:5), a name Jewish and Syriac Christians long kept. Matthew uses it to mean a man from Nazareth, but no Old Testament verse contains ‘He will be called a Nazarene’, and Matthew says prophets, plural. The main proposals are a wordplay on netser, branch, in Isaiah 11:1; an echo of nazir, a Nazirite consecrated to God (Judges 13:5), though Jesus was not one; and the theme of the despised Messiah, since Nazareth was an obscure village (John 1:46).

christ:
Matthew shows Jesus as the true king, the true Israel, and the one to whom the nations come. The chief priests and scribes quote Micah: “But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.” In Micah that ruler's “origins are of old, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2), and he will “stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD” (Micah 5:4). Jesus is that shepherd-king from David's town, and the Aramaic Targum of Micah 5:1 already named him Messiah. Matthew changes Micah's “small among the clans of Judah” to by no means least: the birth of this ruler has made the little town great.

The quotation “Out of Egypt I called My Son” comes from Hosea 11:1, where it looks back to the exodus and speaks of Israel as God's son, as God had called Israel “My firstborn son” in Exodus 4:22. Matthew is not claiming that Hosea predicted this event. He is saying that Jesus relives Israel's story as the Son in whom Israel's sonship reaches its goal. Hosea goes on to lament that the more God called Israel, the farther they went (Hosea 11:2); the Son who now comes out of Egypt will be obedient where Israel was not. Matthew follows the Hebrew here, since the Greek Septuagint reads ‘his children’.

Jeremiah's picture of Rachel weeping for her children comes from a chapter about exile that turns at once to hope: “Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears,” and “Then your children will return from the land of the enemy” (Jeremiah 31:16), a chapter that goes on to promise the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Matthew places the grief of Bethlehem's mothers inside that same promise, and Jesus will pour out the blood of that covenant (26:28). Nazareth completes the picture. Whether Matthew hears in it the Branch from Jesse's stump (Isaiah 11:1) or the despised and rejected servant (Isaiah 53:3), the Messiah grows up in obscurity. The Magi's worship anticipates the end of the Gospel, when the risen Jesus sends his disciples to all nations. From his cradle to his cross, the King of the Jews is received by outsiders and rejected by the powerful.
interpretation:
The Magi fascinated the early church. Ignatius of Antioch (To the Ephesians 19, around 110) describes a star brighter than all the stars, at which the old order of magic was dissolved. Justin (Dialogue 78, around 160) says the Magi came from Arabia and that Jesus was born in a cave near Bethlehem. Tertullian (Against Marcion 3.13) called them almost kings, and Origen favored their number as three, taken from the gifts, and linked them with Balaam's star oracle (Against Celsus, book 1). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.9.2) read the gifts as naming Jesus king, God, and one who would die. John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 6, around 390) argued that the star was no ordinary star but a power that moved and stopped as no star does, and that it gave no support to astrology. Augustine and Leo the Great preached on the feast of the Epiphany year after year, reading the Magi as the firstfruits of the Gentiles. By the sixth century the Magi had names, Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar, which appear in the Latin chronicle called the Excerpta Latina Barbari, and relics said to be theirs were moved from Milan to Cologne in 1164, where they rest in the Shrine of the Three Kings.

Epiphany (6 January) celebrates the Magi in the West and the baptism of Christ in the East. The feast of the Holy Innocents falls on 28 December in the West and 29 December in the Orthodox calendar. The sixteenth-century Coventry Carol, from the Pageant of the Shearmen and Tailors (in a text dated 1534), is a lullaby sung by Bethlehem's mothers. Painters made the chapter their own: Giotto's Adoration in the Arena Chapel in Padua (about 1305) gives the star a comet's tail, Gentile da Fabriano's Adoration of the Magi (1423) makes their train a royal procession, Pieter Bruegel the Elder set the Massacre of the Innocents in a snowy Flemish village (about 1565 to 1567), and Peter Paul Rubens painted its violence in full (about 1611 to 1612). Gian Carlo Menotti's opera Amahl and the Night Visitors (1951) was written for television. Johannes Kepler, having watched a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in 1603, proposed that a similar conjunction in 7 BC was the star, and the astronomical search has continued since.

Jewish interpretation reads Hosea 11:1 of Israel, as Hosea's own context requires, and Christian interpreters have long admitted that Matthew's use is typological rather than predictive; Jerome discussed it in his commentary on Hosea. Modern critical scholarship has read the chapter as haggadic midrash, a retelling of Scripture in narrative form: Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) saw a pre-Matthean story modeled on Moses, and Robert Gundry's commentary (1982) argued that Matthew freely embellished his sources, a view that led to Gundry's departure from the Evangelical Theological Society in 1983. Others, including R. T. France and Craig Keener, defend the story's historical core. The Magi have also been claimed by outsiders to the church as a sign that God speaks beyond its walls, and by the church as a sign that all such seeking ends at the feet of Christ.
text:
Micah 5:2 in English Bibles is Micah 5:1 in the Hebrew text, because the Hebrew counts the last verse of English chapter 4 as 5:1. Matthew's quotation matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly: he writes by no means least where Micah has small, rulers where the Hebrew has clans (the two words differ by vowels only), and adds the shepherd line from 2 Samuel 5:2. At Hosea 11:1 Matthew follows the Hebrew ‘my son’; the Septuagint reads ‘his children’, which could not have served his point.

In verse 18 the King James Version reads ‘lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning’, with an extra noun found in later manuscripts and in the Septuagint of Jeremiah; the earliest manuscripts have only weeping and great mourning. The phrase en tē anatolē in verses 2 and 9 is translated ‘in the east’ (KJV, BSB, NIV) or ‘at its rising’ (NRSV; the ESV has ‘when it rose’), a choice of interpretation rather than of text. The small differences in the dream verbs (appeared, appears) in verses 13 and 19 do not change the sense.

teach.big: The true King of the Jews is received with joy by Gentile seekers and hunted by the powerful, and God protects and guides him through danger and exile as he relives and fulfills Israel's story.

outline.t: Seekers from far outside Israel come asking for the King, and God meets them through the only light they have.
Jerusalem's experts can quote the Scripture that points to the Messiah and still not go; knowing where Christ is differs from coming to him.
Herod speaks the language of worship while planning murder; power that feels threatened by Christ disguises its intentions.
The Magi's worship is joyful, costly, and obedient: they rejoice, fall down, give their treasures, and go home by another way.
The Son of God becomes a refugee, and like Israel he is called out of Egypt; God protects him through flight, not by removing danger.
Scripture does not hide the cost of evil: Herod's rage kills children, and Matthew lets Rachel weep inside Jeremiah's promise of hope.
God guides step by step through dreams and circumstances, and the King grows up in a despised village, as the prophets foresaw.

teach.pitfalls:
Common teaching borrows more from Christmas cards than from Matthew. The text does not say there were three Magi or that they were kings, and they came to a house, not the manger, probably months after the birth. Correcting these gently can open the text afresh, but do not make the sermon a list of corrections. Avoid presenting the Magi as endorsing astrology; Matthew shows God meeting them where they were and then leading them by Scripture.

Do not rush past the massacre to make a point about Jesus' safety, and do not say God sent the massacre to fulfill prophecy; Matthew's change of wording at verse 17 guards against exactly that. Avoid treating out of Egypt I called my Son as a crude prediction that Hosea did not intend; explaining typology honestly strengthens rather than weakens Matthew's case. Finally, the refugee theme is real and worth teaching, but tying the text to a single policy position narrows it; its first claim is about who Jesus is and what kind of king he will be.
teach.pastoral: Verses 16 to 18 will reach parents who have lost a child, and people who have lost children to violence or war. Let Rachel's weeping stand before offering comfort, as Matthew does, and do not suggest that the loss served a purpose. Jeremiah's promise that follows (Jeremiah 31:16-17) and the hope of the resurrection can be offered, but gently. The flight to Egypt also speaks to refugees and to families who have fled danger; the holy family knew what it is to live as foreigners. The story of seekers who come from outside the church and are welcomed will encourage those who feel they arrived late or from far away.

hard.q: Did the massacre of the innocents and the visit of the Magi really happen?
hard.a:
The objection is serious. Josephus describes Herod's crimes in great detail across books 15 to 17 of the Antiquities, yet says nothing of Bethlehem, and no other ancient source does either, apart from Macrobius's late and confused report. Luke's account of the infancy sends the family from Bethlehem to the temple in Jerusalem and home to Nazareth (Luke 2:22-39) with no flight to Egypt. The story closely follows the Moses legend as Jewish tradition told it, with a king warned by scribes, a massacre of boys, a child saved, and a return after the tyrant's death. On these grounds Raymond Brown (1977), E. P. Sanders (The Historical Figure of Jesus, 1993), and Geza Vermes (The Nativity: History and Legend, 2006) judged the chapter largely a theological narrative rather than a historical report, and Robert Gundry (1982) read it as Matthew's midrashic expansion of simpler tradition.

Those who defend its historical core reply that the silence of Josephus weighs less than it seems. Bethlehem was small, and the number of boys under two may have been a dozen or two (R. T. France, Novum Testamentum, 1979; Paul Maier, 1998), too few to be noticed beside the executions of Herod's own sons, the killing of the Pharisees who opposed him, and his order to murder the nation's leaders at his death. The act fits his character exactly. Luke and Matthew each select events without claiming to tell everything, and Luke's summary need not exclude a flight. That the story echoes Moses shows how Matthew understood it, not necessarily that he invented it, since events can be told in the shape of older ones; Craig Keener and France make this case. On the Magi, the visit of the Armenian king Tiridates to Nero with magi in AD 66 shows that eastern sages did travel to pay homage to kings. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture have mostly defended the events as history, while differing on how much Matthew shaped their telling; the historical question cannot be settled by the evidence now available.

hard.q: Why would God protect Jesus but allow the children of Bethlehem to be killed?
hard.a:
The objection is as old as faith itself and is not only a skeptic's. The protest against the suffering of children has its most famous modern form in Ivan Karamazov's speech in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880): no future harmony could justify the tears of a single tortured child. Applied here, the question is sharp. An angel warns one father and not the others; the Son of God escapes while other sons die because of him.

Matthew does not explain it, and he does not make the massacre small. He lets Rachel weep and refuse to be comforted. Several things can be said honestly. First, Matthew consistently presents the evil as Herod's, and at verse 17 he avoids saying that it happened in order to fulfill Scripture, as he says of other events. Second, the rescued child is not exempt from what Herod did; he will himself be killed by the rulers of his people and of Rome, sharing the fate of the innocent rather than escaping it for good. Third, Jeremiah's words about Rachel belong to a chapter that promises the children's return and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:16-17, 31-34), and Christians have read that hope as fulfilled in the resurrection. The Western church has honored the children of Bethlehem as the first martyrs for Christ at least since the fifth century. None of this answers every question about why God permits such evil, a question Scripture itself raises in the Psalms, Job, and Lamentations, but Matthew does not pretend the question away.

observe: Trace the four places in this chapter and the Scripture Matthew attaches to each. What part of Israel's history does each recall?
What does Herod say he wants to do in verse 8, and what does he actually do? Compare with what the Magi do in verses 10 and 11.
How many times is someone warned in a dream in this chapter, and how does each respond?
interpret: Why might Matthew tell the story in a way that recalls Moses and the exodus? What does it suggest about who Jesus is?
Hosea 11:1 originally spoke of Israel. In what sense can Matthew say it was fulfilled in Jesus?
Why does Matthew write ‘then was fulfilled’ at verse 17 rather than ‘in order to fulfill’, as at verses 15 and 23?
apply: The scribes knew where the Messiah would be born but stayed home. Where does knowing about Christ risk becoming a substitute for coming to him in your life?
Herod saw a child as a threat to his power. What in your life feels threatened by Jesus' kingship?
How should the story of the holy family's flight shape the way you treat refugees and strangers where you live?
